title: The Queue Voices
heading: Voices, round 2: an English tannoy
intro: Your note: the tannoy sounded American, not English. Four new designed voices, each tied to an English region (Surrey, London, Kent, the Midlands); I can't judge an accent by ear, so this pick is yours. Also here: the one free-to-use real recording (it says 'number one'). The Primark recording is Primark's own, so it's off limits.

groups.title: The tannoy, English
groups.line: tannoy-c: An English woman of about 40 from Surrey, with a crisp southern English accent, the calm recorded voice of a shop's queue system, who speaks plainly. / tannoy-d: An English woman of about 35 from London, with a standard southern English accent and a bright, neutral tone, a recorded store announcement voice, who speaks plainly. / tannoy-e: An English woman of about 45 from Kent, with a clear, received pronunciation accent, an automated public announcement voice, who speaks plainly. / tannoy-f: An English woman of about 30 from the Midlands, with a soft English accent, a recorded queue announcement voice, who speaks plainly.

opts.label: the real recording (CC0, Freesound, nigelcoop): says 'Cashier number ONE, please'

groups.title: The tannoy
groups.line: tannoy-a: A calm, flat, automated-sounding British woman of about 40, who speaks plainly. / tannoy-b: A polite, slightly bored British woman of about 50, an announcer's even voice, who speaks plainly.  My pick: tannoy-a (overrule here).

groups.title: The pensioner
groups.line: pensioner-a: A woman of about 75 from the south of England, with a warm, slightly creaky voice, who speaks plainly. / pensioner-b: A woman of about 78 from Yorkshire, with a dry, firm voice, who speaks plainly.  My pick: pensioner-b (overrule here).

groups.title: The cashier (BadCode, dressed as a 60-year-old Karen)
groups.line: cashier-a: A woman of about 60 from the Home Counties, with a clipped, stern, slightly nasal voice, who speaks plainly. / cashier-b: A man of about 60 from the south of England, with a dry, deadpan, measured voice, who speaks plainly.  My pick: cashier-a (overrule here).
